concept.name: Price discovery
concept.definition: The process by which markets incorporate information into prices through the interaction of buy and sell interest, producing transaction and quotation prices that reflect participants' aggregate assessment of value. Auctions, continuous order books, and dealer quotes are all price discovery mechanisms; opening and closing crosses are explicitly designed as price discovery facilities.
concept.intuition: Nobody sets the price — it emerges from thousands of orders colliding, each carrying someone's information and opinion.
concept.mechanics: Orders express information and willingness to trade; matching converts that flow into trades and quotes, and the published prices feed back as reference points (for valuation, derivatives settlement, and collateral) that shape subsequent order flow. Fragmentation, dark trading, and delayed reporting can weaken the public component of the process.
concept.failure_modes: Price discovery degrades when trading is one-sided (panics, no-bid markets), when liquidity is withdrawn faster than information can be absorbed (flash crashes), or when most flow moves to non-displayed venues, hollowing out public quotes.
concept.misconceptions: Discovered prices are not 'correct' prices — they are market-clearing prices conditional on who showed up to trade; efficient-market claims about their information content are hypotheses, not guarantees.
concept.example: After a surprise earnings release, pre-market orders push a stock's indicative opening price from $95 to $102; the opening auction aggregates that interest into a single new opening print.

citations.source: SEC, Concept Release on Equity Market Structure (Release No. 34-61358)
